title: CEF Sentinel
description: Business dashboard: CEF premiums/discounts, z-scores and macro traffic lights. Data is informational only; intraday discounts are ESTIMATES (yesterday's NAV). Not investment advice.

panels.title: HY credit spread (ICE BofA OAS)
panels.description:
Extra yield that high-yield ('junk') corporate bonds pay over US Treasuries — THE credit-stress thermometer. Widening = fear and falling bond prices (the buying window for credit CEFs may be opening); tight = calm, or complacency.

READ IT WITH CARE: FRED only publishes a rolling ~3-year window of this series (ICE licence), so 'high' and 'low' here are relative to a very short memory. Today's ~2.8% sits around the 26th percentile of those 3 years — which sounds ordinary — but measured against decades it is historically TIGHT. The chart below (Baa spread, back to 2007) supplies the missing scale.

targets.rawSql: SELECT obs_date::timestamptz AS "time", value FROM silver.macro_series WHERE series_id = 'BAMLH0A0HYM2' ORDER BY 1

panels.title: EUR/USD (ECB fixing)
panels.description: Official daily ECB fixing (~16:00 CET). Personal band: 1.10 - 1.20; outside the band = act (display reference only).

targets.rawSql: SELECT obs_date::timestamptz AS "time", value FROM silver.macro_series WHERE series_id = 'EURUSD_ECB' ORDER BY 1

panels.title: Buffett indicator (W5000 / GDP)
panels.description: Total US market cap proxy vs nominal GDP. What matters is the level vs its own history, not the absolute number.

targets.rawSql: SELECT obs_date::timestamptz AS "time", buffett_pct FROM gold.buffett_indicator ORDER BY 1

panels.title: VIX

targets.rawSql: SELECT trading_date::timestamptz AS "time", close FROM silver.prices_daily WHERE ticker = '^VIX' ORDER BY 1

panels.description:
The market's 'fear gauge': the volatility the options market EXPECTS in the S&P 500 over the next 30 days. It is a forecast of turbulence, not a direction — it rises in crashes because violent moves are expected, not because prices must fall.

Rough guide: under 15 = calm · 15-20 = normal · 20-30 = nervous · above 30 = fear · above 50 = panic (seen in 2008 and March 2020).

WHY IT MATTERS HERE: fear is what widens CEF discounts. When the VIX spikes, retail holders sell closed-end funds faster than the underlying bonds move, so price falls further than NAV and the discount opens — which is exactly the anomaly this dashboard hunts. A calm VIX with wide discounts is a different (and rarer) signal than a panicked VIX with wide discounts.

It mean-reverts hard: spikes are violent and short-lived, so a high reading is a moment to look, not a level that lasts.

panels.title: Is today's spread normal? - long-run context (Baa proxy for the panel above)
panels.description:
The context the panel above cannot give. Moody's Baa corporate bond yield minus the 10-year Treasury: the same idea as the HY spread (what investors demand for taking credit risk) but on investment-grade bonds — and, crucially, NOT licence-restricted, so it reaches back to 2007 instead of 3 years.

The two are not interchangeable: Baa is higher quality, so its LEVELS are lower than high yield. What transfers is the SHAPE — where we sit relative to calm and to crisis.

The flat line is today's level, drawn across the whole window so you can see at a glance whether now is historically calm or stressed. For reference, this spread peaked at 6.16% in the 2008 crisis; today it is around 1.6%.

Use the time picker (top right) to widen or narrow the window — zoom out to include 2008 and 2020 for the full picture.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT obs_date::timestamptz AS "time",
       value AS "Baa - 10Y spread",
       (SELECT value FROM silver.macro_series
         WHERE series_id = 'BAA10Y'
         ORDER BY obs_date DESC LIMIT 1) AS "Today"
  FROM silver.macro_series
 WHERE series_id = 'BAA10Y'
   AND $__timeFilter(obs_date::timestamptz)
 ORDER BY 1

panels.title: CEF universe - now (sorted by z-score: most anomalously cheap first)

targets.rawSql: SELECT s.ticker AS "CEF", s.price AS "Price", s.nav AS "NAV", s.nav_date::text AS "NAV date", s.nav_quality AS "NAV quality", round(s.premium_discount * 100, 2) AS "Prem/Disc %", s.estado AS "Status", round(y.yield_ttm_on_price_pct, 2) AS "Yield %", y.n_dist_ttm AS "Payments/yr", round(s.zscore::numeric, 2) AS "Z-score", s.n_obs AS "Obs (1y)", s.zscore_date::text AS "Z-score date", s.zscore_band AS "Signal" FROM gold.cef_snapshot s LEFT JOIN gold.yield_ttm y ON y.ticker = s.ticker ORDER BY s.zscore ASC NULLS LAST

options.content:
### Reading the CEF universe table

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **CEF** | Fund name and ticker. The universe is config-driven (tickers.yaml), not hardcoded. |
| **Price** | Latest market price per share - unadjusted daily close (the real on-screen price). |
| **NAV** | Net Asset Value per share published by the fund (via CEFConnect): what the portfolio is actually worth. |
| **NAV date** | Date of the NAV shown. Published once a day after the close, so it normally lags price by one trading day. |
| **NAV quality** | Freshness computed in SQL: *estimado* = up to 4 calendar days old (normal - weekends/holidays); *rancio* = older, the NAV scraper is likely failing. |
| **Prem/Disc %** | (Price - NAV) / NAV. Negative = discount (you pay less than the portfolio is worth), positive = premium. Gradient over +/-15%. |
| **Status** | The sign of Prem/Disc % as a word: Premium / Discount / Par. Some funds (e.g. PIMCO) habitually trade at persistent premiums. |
| **Yield %** | Distribution yield on PRICE, trailing 12 months: everything paid in the last 12m divided by today's price. Deliberately NOT colored: a very high yield can signal distress, not a gift - see the yield table below for the NAV yield and the cut signal. |
| **Payments/yr** | Distributions paid in the trailing 12 months (~12 = monthly payer, ~4 = quarterly). |
| **Z-score** | How unusual today's premium/discount is versus this fund's OWN last year, in standard deviations. 0 = its normal level; -2 = unusually cheap (roughly the cheapest ~2% of days); +2 = unusually expensive. Big negative z-score with enough observations = the anomaly worth investigating. |
| **Obs (1y)** | Daily observations behind the z-score (max ~252 trading sessions). Low count = young series - read the z-score with caution. |
| **Z-score date** | Date of the last daily observation used in the z-score (updates after each NAV ingest). |

panels.title: Yield & distributions (TTM) - sorted by yield on price
panels.description: Distribution yield per CEF from gold.yield_ttm. 'Yield on price' = what a buyer today collects (12 months of distributions / current price). 'Yield on NAV' = what the portfolio must actually earn to sustain the payout - the gap between the two IS the discount. 'Yield current' = last distribution annualized at the fund's own payment cadence; below the TTM yield means the fund recently CUT its distribution - the event that historically precedes discount blowouts. 'Dist trend' compares the current annualized rate vs what was actually paid over 12 months: negative = cutting, ~0 = stable. High yield is NOT automatically good: it can signal distress - read it together with the discount z-score above.

targets.rawSql: SELECT ticker AS "CEF", round(yield_ttm_on_price_pct, 2) AS "Yield on price %", round(yield_ttm_on_nav_pct, 2) AS "Yield on NAV %", round(yield_current_pct, 2) AS "Yield current %", round((yield_current_pct / yield_ttm_on_price_pct - 1) * 100, 1) AS "Dist trend %", dist_ttm AS "Paid 12m $", n_dist_ttm AS "Payments (1y)", last_amount AS "Last dist $", last_ex_date::text AS "Last ex-date" FROM gold.yield_ttm ORDER BY yield_ttm_on_price_pct DESC

panels.title: Stocks & ETFs watchlist
panels.description: Equities and ETFs from the watchlist - real USD prices. Green = up on the day (standard market semantics, unlike the discount table).

targets.rawSql: WITH r AS (SELECT ticker, trading_date, close, lag(close) OVER (PARTITION BY ticker ORDER BY trading_date) AS prev, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY ticker ORDER BY trading_date DESC) AS rn FROM silver.prices_daily WHERE ticker NOT IN (SELECT DISTINCT ticker FROM silver.navs) AND ticker NOT LIKE '^%' AND ticker NOT LIKE '%=X') SELECT ticker AS "Asset", trading_date::text AS "Date", close AS "Last price", round((close / prev - 1) * 100, 2) AS "Day %" FROM r WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY ticker

panels.title: Indexes & FX
panels.description: Index levels are POINTS and EUR/USD is a rate - deliberately no currency symbol here (a $ on the VIX would be a lie).

targets.rawSql: WITH r AS (SELECT ticker, trading_date, close, lag(close) OVER (PARTITION BY ticker ORDER BY trading_date) AS prev, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY ticker ORDER BY trading_date DESC) AS rn FROM silver.prices_daily WHERE ticker LIKE '^%' OR ticker LIKE '%=X') SELECT ticker AS "Index / pair", trading_date::text AS "Date", close AS "Last level", round((close / prev - 1) * 100, 2) AS "Day %" FROM r WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY ticker

panels.title: Signal backtest - what happened after z-score crossed below -2
panels.description: For each historical crossing of z-score <= -2 (with >=126 obs), the discount reversion and price move at +1/+3/+6 months. Read with the caveat panel: the sample is dominated by the 2026-03 credit sell-off.

targets.rawSql: SELECT horizon_months AS "Horizon (months)", n_signals_realized AS "Signals (matured)", n_signals_total AS "Signals (total)", round(reversion_hit_rate * 100, 1) AS "Discount reverted %", round(price_up_hit_rate * 100, 1) AS "Price up %", round(avg_price_return * 100, 2) AS "Avg price return %" FROM gold.signal_backtest_summary ORDER BY horizon_months

panels.title: How to read the backtest (honest caveats)

options.content:
**Thesis under test:** when a CEF's discount becomes anomalously wide (z-score crosses below **-2**), does the discount *revert* (narrow) and the *price* rise over the next 1 / 3 / 6 months?

- **Discount reverted %** / **Price up %** = share of *matured* signals where it happened.
- **Sampling caveat:** so far ~half the signals come from the **2026-03 credit sell-off**, where nearly the whole universe crossed -2 at once and rebounded together. Those are **correlated**, not independent - a high hit rate today reflects *one episode*, not a proven edge.
- **+6m has not matured yet** (needs 6 months of forward data). The sample grows with every accumulated trading day.
- *Mechanical note:* a z-score is a deviation from a 1-year moving average, so some reversion is built in. **Price return** is the more independent signal.

panels.title: Composite score - OPINIONATED, read the caveats first
panels.description: A convenience ranking, not a signal. The weights are an opinion expressed as arithmetic; they have no backtest behind them. The only thing here with evidence is the z-score, and even that is dominated by one cluster of correlated signals (see the backtest panel). Components are shown next to the total on purpose.

targets.rawSql:
-- Score compuesto -- OPINABLE A PROPOSITO. Ver la nota del panel.
--
-- Los pesos viven AQUI, en la query del panel, y no en una vista de gold, y no
-- es pereza: es donde mas visible resulta que son una OPINION. Cualquiera que
-- abra el panel los lee. En gold quedarian con rango de verdad de negocio, que
-- es justo lo que no tienen. Contradice la #26 ("la semantica vive en gold") y
-- el contrapeso es deliberado.
--
-- Cada componente se normaliza a percentil DENTRO del universo (PERCENT_RANK):
-- comparar un z-score con un yield en porcentaje seria sumar peras y manzanas,
-- y cualquier escalado absoluto exigiria elegir constantes todavia mas
-- arbitrarias que los pesos. El percentil solo afirma "de estos 19, este esta
-- arriba o abajo" -- que es exactamente lo que un ranking puede sostener.
WITH base AS (
    SELECT
        s.ticker,
        s.premium_discount,
        s.zscore,
        s.nav_quality,
        y.yield_ttm_on_price_pct AS yield_pct,
        -- ¿Recorte de distribucion en los ultimos 12 meses? En un CEF de credito
        -- el yield ES la tesis, asi que un recorte reciente pesa en contra por
        -- mucho que el descuento se haya abierto -- a menudo se abre POR el
        -- recorte: el mercado ya lo sabe y el descuento no es una ganga.
        EXISTS (
            SELECT 1 FROM gold.distribution_cuts c
            WHERE c.ticker = s.ticker AND c.ex_date >= current_date - 365
        ) AS recorte_reciente
    FROM gold.cef_snapshot s
    LEFT JOIN gold.yield_ttm y ON y.ticker = s.ticker
    -- Sin historia suficiente el z-score no significa nada (mismo umbral de
    -- 126 sesiones que usa el backtest de la 8 1/2 para admitir una senal).
    WHERE s.n_obs >= 126
),
percentiles AS (
    SELECT
        *,
        -- OJO CON EL SENTIDO: PERCENT_RANK() da 0 a la PRIMERA fila del orden,
        -- asi que el ORDER BY va al REVES de lo que uno escribiria por instinto.
        -- Las dos primeras versiones de esta query tenian un componente
        -- invertido cada una, y las dos producian una tabla perfectamente
        -- plausible: rankings creibles con la senal del reves. Solo se ve
        -- ejecutandola y mirando los extremos.
        --   zscore DESC  -> el mas NEGATIVO (mas barato frente a SU PROPIA
        --                   historia, la tesis del proyecto) queda el ultimo
        --                   del orden y se lleva el percentil 100.
        PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY zscore DESC)::numeric   AS p_zscore,
        --   yield ASC    -> el yield MAS ALTO queda el ultimo y se lleva el 100.
        PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY yield_pct ASC)::numeric AS p_yield
    FROM base
)
SELECT
    ticker                                        AS "CEF",
    -- Positivos: dos componentes que suman 1. Negativos: penalizaciones
    -- explicitas, no pesos -- son banderas rojas, no ejes de comparacion.
    -- El NAV NO puntua en positivo (a media sesion casi todos estan
    -- 'estimado', asi que premiarlo solo deflactaria el score de todos por
    -- igual sin cambiar el orden); solo RESTA cuando esta mal de verdad.
    round(100 * (0.60 * p_zscore + 0.40 * p_yield)
          - CASE WHEN recorte_reciente THEN 15 ELSE 0 END
          - CASE WHEN nav_quality IN ('rancio', 'sospechoso') THEN 10 ELSE 0 END
    , 1)                                          AS "Score",
    -- Los COMPONENTES, siempre al lado del total: sin ellos un ranking es un
    -- oraculo. Con ellos se ve POR QUE puntua alto, que es lo unico util.
    round(zscore, 2)                              AS "z-score",
    round(100 * p_zscore)                         AS "z pctl",
    round(yield_pct, 1)                           AS "Yield %",
    round(100 * p_yield)                          AS "yield pctl",
    CASE WHEN recorte_reciente THEN 'yes (-15)' ELSE 'no' END AS "Cut 12m",
    CASE WHEN nav_quality IN ('rancio', 'sospechoso')
         THEN nav_quality || ' (-10)' ELSE nav_quality END    AS "NAV quality",
    round(100 * premium_discount, 2)              AS "Discount %"
FROM percentiles
ORDER BY 2 DESC

panels.title: How to read the score (and why you probably shouldn't)

options.content:
**This is the most arguable panel in the project, and it is here on purpose.**

`Score = 60% z-score percentile + 40% yield percentile - 15 if distribution cut in 12m - 10 if NAV rancio/sospechoso`

- **The weights are an opinion.** Why 60/40 and not 50/50? No reason that survives scrutiny. Nothing was optimised or backtested to pick them. A composite score always looks more rigorous than its inputs justify — that is precisely the trap, and the reason the components are shown next to the total: so you read *why* something ranks high instead of trusting the number.
- **Percentiles are relative to these 19 funds only.** A score of 100 means "cheapest of this list", never "cheap". If the whole credit market is expensive, the top of this table is still expensive.
- **It says nothing about *why* a fund is cheap.** A wide discount often reflects something real that the market already knows — leverage, credit quality, an upcoming cut. The cut penalty is a crude proxy for that, not a substitute for reading the fund.
- **The z-score is the only component with any evidence behind it**, and the backtest panel above spells out its limits (43 signals, half of them from the same March 2026 sell-off).

*Not investment advice. See the disclaimer in the README.*
